plan.topic: Zepbound (tirzepatide) single-dose vial vs single-dose pen: what's in the box, what each device asks you to do, storage, injection sites and disposal, taken only from the US prescribing information and each device's own Instructions for Use
plan.angle:
A side-by-side device how-to, 9–11 min.

**Gate:** script it only if the Lilly Zepbound single-dose vial IFU and single-dose pen IFU both load at their own URLs with readable revised dates. Read the Zepbound PI date on DailyMed (sections 2, 3, 16 and 17 only). If the vial IFU doesn't load, drop L4 and ship the next ready video in the queue.

**Opening:** sentence 1 names Zepbound and answers the question. Something like: 'If your Zepbound comes as a vial instead of a pen, it's the same medicine, tirzepatide, but you use a separate syringe and needle, and the vial's instructions add steps the pen does for you.' The second payoff at 15–30 s is the first concrete vial step from the vial IFU. Say early that KwikPens have their own leaflet: follow the one in your box and ask a pharmacist to show you.

**Chapters, named as the questions people search:**
1. What's in the box with each one? Only what each IFU lists.
2. What does the pen do that the vial doesn't? Pen steps from the pen IFU (unlock, place flat, press, the clicks, hold).
3. Using the vial: the steps in vial-IFU wording (supplies, wiping the stopper, the syringe steps). Never speak or show syringe markings, amounts or doses. Say the vial is single-dose only if the IFU says so, and quote its line about leftover medicine exactly.
4. Where to inject and rotating sites, in PI or IFU wording.
5. Storage and time out of the fridge, with the exact limits from PI section 16 and each IFU.
6. Disposal: the IFU wording plus the FDA sharps guidance, 'follow your local rules', and never loose sharps in household trash.
7. When to call: injection-site reactions at 6–8% by dose vs about 2% on placebo (PI 6.1, with the population on the card), the full allergy emergency card, then the fixed don't-stop line.

**Rules:**
- No cost, coverage, Medicare, switching or 'which is better' talk.
- No technique beyond the IFUs, and no dose, missed-dose or titration content.
- Re-hook every 45–75 s. Land the last new fact before 80%, and keep lists to 3 items at most.
- One subscribe ask, after the chapter 3 payoff.
- 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line are spoken and shown on screen.
- Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' The publisher links the pen how-to video (qiLPt1hHGL0).
- Thumbnail: 'VIAL OR PEN?' with one calm labelled character holding both devices. No body imagery.

plan.why: A queued search-demand device how-to built on primary label and IFU sources, so it should pass the fact-check first time. It doesn't repeat the dropped topics or today's Shorts, and it gives the pen and injection Shorts a new link target.

package.description:
Stop using Zepbound and get medical help right away if you have swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat, problems breathing or swallowing, severe rash or itching, fainting or feeling dizzy, or a very rapid heartbeat. For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.

Quick answer: a Zepbound single-dose vial and single-dose pen hold the same tirzepatide. The pen is prefilled with the needle built in. The single-dose vial needs a separate syringe and needle (ask your prescriber or pharmacist which ones) and is used once, then thrown away with any medicine left inside. KwikPen or multiple-dose vial? Follow the leaflet in your box.

The unboxing moment follows right after. The second payoff, the first vial step from the vial IFU, lands at 15–30 s. Early scope lines send KwikPen and multiple-dose vial users to their own leaflets. A one-sentence open loop pays off in the storage chapter.

factcheck.summary:
The script passes. Its claims match the Zepbound US prescribing information, which DailyMed shows as revised 16 Nov 2026. I confirmed these points against it:
- Four presentations: single-dose pen, single-dose vial, multiple-dose vial and KwikPen. This supports the scope lines in s4 and s4b.
- Both indications, including moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity.
- Injection-site reactions: 6%, 8% and 8% on 5, 10 and 15 mg, versus 2% on placebo, in the pooled weight-reduction trials.
- Storage: 2–8°C (36–46°F), do not freeze, keep in the carton to protect from light, and a single-dose pen or vial may be kept unrefrigerated up to 30°C (86°F) for up to 21 days.
- Injection sites and rotation.

The pen steps (lock ring, purple button, two clicks, gray plunger, 2 inches from the belly button), the vial points (syringe and needle not included, throw the vial away after one use even with medicine left, sharps disposal) and the allergy list in the Medication Guide also matched secondary copies of the leaflets. So did the FDA sharps guidance (about three-quarters full, content current as of 10 Aug 2023). Dana is clearly made up and isn't shamed. The safety lines, the don't-stop line and the prescriber line are all there, and there's no dosing, no syringe markings and no switching advice.

**Limits on what I checked:** WebFetch couldn't read the text of the three Lilly PDFs (pen leaflet, vial leaflet, Medication Guide). All three URLs answered (300 KB, 620 KB and 193 KB), but the IFU and Medication Guide wording is checked against search excerpts and secondary pages that repeat the leaflet text, not the PDFs themselves. For the same reason I couldn't read the leaflets' own revision dates. One more thing: the fetch tool's summaries of DailyMed changed between calls, and one included a 28-day storage claim that the verbatim quote didn't. The numbers above come from the verbatim quotes, where I could get them.

The four fixes below are wording and citation polish. None of them changes a fact.

issues.claim: Everything here comes from the US prescribing information and each device's own Instructions for Use, with no amounts and no doses.
issues.problem: This isn't fully true: s54 and s55 use FDA sharps-disposal guidance (S5), which is neither the label nor a leaflet.
issues.fix: Narration: "Everything here comes from the US prescribing information, each device's own Instructions for Use and the FDA's sharps guidance, with no amounts and no doses." Spell out the contraction for the voice engine: "each device's" is a possessive, so keep it. Source_ids: add "S5".

issues.claim: Step three: press and hold the purple injection button. You will hear a loud click, which means the injection has started.
issues.problem: The pen leaflet's step 3 is "press and hold for up to 10 seconds". Leaving out the time limit takes away a cue viewers use to know when to stop.
issues.fix: Narration: "Step three: press and hold the purple injection button for up to ten seconds. You will hear a loud click, which means the injection has started." On-screen text: "3: Press and hold (up to 10 s)"

issues.claim: S2 Medication Guide URL is the same DailyMed page as S1

issues: Generic shipping-box visual doesn't show either device (vial or pen), weakening the curiosity payoff since the image doesn't match the question
Less specific/relatable than the other two options
Red X badge on VIAL and green check badge on PEN implies vial is 'wrong' and pen is 'approved/better', a judgment the neutral title doesn't support and that could mislead before the viewer watches
Slightly busier layout with two characters, VS text, and badges competing for attention at phone size
Capsule-shaped pen character could be briefly mistaken for the vial itself at a glance, though the text clarifies quickly

thumbnail.reasoning: All three keep the hedge neutral (none states an answer, so no hard-cap triggers). #0's box-and-question-mark art doesn't actually depict a vial or pen, so it undercuts its own headline and feels generic/replaceable with any 'what's in the box' thumbnail — weaker specific curiosity for this exact topic. #1 is clean and legible but the red X / green check badges under VIAL and PEN visually imply a right-answer/wrong-answer judgment that the title ('What's Different?') never claims, which risks a misleading first impression even though the words themselves don't give anything away. #2 ('FOUND A VIAL? EXPECTED A PEN?') is the most emotionally specific and relatable — it mirrors the real moment someone unboxes their refill and is confused, which is exactly the audience this video serves (Zepbound users navigating the vial supply). The character's shocked face matches the surprised tone of the text, the two-line headline plus subtext is clean and reads in under a second at phone size, and it doesn't imply any answer or bias. That combination of strong, honest curiosity pull and clean legibility makes it the best pick.
